## Everything About The Luteal Phase.

The luteal phase is the part of your cycle after ovulation. Here is what to know about it.

### How long should it be?

Usually 11 to 17 days. Under 10 days is called a short luteal phase and may make implantation harder.

### Why does it matter?

After ovulation the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone. Progesterone thickens the uterine lining so an embryo can implant. If progesterone is too low or falls too early, the lining sheds before implantation can happen.

### How do you measure it?

Count from the day after ovulation to the day before your next period. Confirming the ovulation day accurately is the hard part — calendar estimates are often several days off. PdG testing confirms it directly.

### What shortens it?

Low progesterone is the main mechanism. Thyroid problems, high prolactin, very low body fat, heavy training loads, and perimenopause all contribute.

### What can you do?

Speak with a clinician if your luteal phase is consistently under 10 days. Treatment depends on the cause and may involve addressing thyroid function or supplementing progesterone.

### Everything About The Luteal Phase.

Tracking a few cycles before drawing conclusions gives a much better picture than a single measurement.
